idiom_name: sealed trait/enum hierarchy + hand-written discriminator mapping (Slick/Doobie)
implementation_notes: Scala's sealed traits and Scala 3 enums give an exhaustive ADT that plays the role of the class hierarchy, but no mainstream Scala persistence library implements STI: Slick is a functional-relational mapping with explicit tables and joins and deliberately does not manage object graphs the way an ORM does, so the discriminator column is mapped by hand and the row is dispatched with a match. JPA/Hibernate can be used from Scala, but the bean/reflection requirements (no-arg constructors, mutable properties) fight case classes and vals, so teams usually keep the tag mapping hand-written and accept either that or a multi-table (JOINED) mapping. Where the hierarchy is closed and small, the enum plus an explicit table definition is the cleaner Scala answer.
code_sketch:
enum Employee:
  case Engineer(id: Long, name: String, language: String)
  case Manager(id: Long, name: String, reports: Int)

def fromRow(kind: String, id: Long, name: String, language: Option[String], reports: Option[Int]): Employee =
  kind match
    case "engineer" => Employee.Engineer(id, name, language.getOrElse(throw MappingError("language")))
    case "manager"  => Employee.Manager(id, name, reports.getOrElse(throw MappingError("reports")))
    case other      => throw MappingError(s"unknown discriminator: $other")
pitfalls: Exhaustive matching protects the dispatch, not the database: the unknown-tag case still needs an explicit branch, and Scala 2 sealed traits require all cases in one compilation unit (Scala 3 enums relax this).

Slick's lifted/plain tables do not know about subtype fields, so a shared nullable column arrives as Option[T] for every case and the ADT cannot express per-subtype non-null invariants without a validation layer.
Java-reflection ORMs on Scala classes need no-arg constructors and mutable vars; case classes with vals silently break Hibernate property access, so mixing JPA with idiomatic Scala types is a trap.
A sum type flattened into one table loses the compiler's help at the boundary: the mapper's Option-extraction is where subtype invariants are enforced, and it must fail loudly.
